newsitem.title: USA: Traders see benefits from CSCE-NYCE merger.
newsitem.headline: Traders see benefits from CSCE-NYCE merger.

text.p: A possible merger between the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange (CSCE) and the New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE) could benefit both exchanges by streamlining operations and increasing trading volume, traders said Friday.

An announcement late Thursday that the two exchanges were exploring a merger deal caused little stir on the trading floor, where the news had long been anticipated, but most brokers viewed the idea favorably.
"I think it's a good thing," said Victor Henriquez, president of Hencorp Becstone in Miami, the coffee-trading arm of New York commission house Refco Inc.
"You should consolidate all of the 'softs'," he added, using the industry term for coffee, sugar, cocoa, cotton and orange juice. "Why have a little bit here and a little bit there?"

The drive toward greater efficiency was seen as crucial by many traders as the New York's biggest futures market, the New York Mercantile Exchange, prepares to move into a new trading facility in lower Manhattan in early July.

Indeed, several traders said NYMEX's widely-publicized move to the new site, where state-of-the-art technology is expected to make trading swifter and easier, may have hastened discussions among CSCE and NYCE board members.
"The NYMEX is moving forward, and moving into new building, while the CSCE and the NYCE never seem to progress," said one trader who requested anonymity.
"The CSCE and the NYCE need to become much more efficient," the trader added. "They are falling behind badly relative to other exchanges."
Currently, all three exchanges share space on a trading floor in the World Trade Center.

Both the CSCE and NYCE have made it known they would be happy to join NYMEX in its new location, but a spokeswoman for the Mercantile Exchange said its offer to lease some 30 percent of its 50,000 square foot trading floor had been turned down by CSCE and NYCE officials.
By taking their merger discussions public, CSCE and NYCE might have been hoping to prod NYMEX to come up with an offer for more space, the trader added.

The three exchanges are continuing negotiations over space in the new NYMEX building, and the NYMEX spokeswoman said she expected the situation to be resolved "one way or the other" within the next year.

In 1995, NYMEX approached the CSCE with a merger bid valued at $50 million. Merger talks barely got off the ground, however, with the CSCE saying it would not consider any offer that did not also include the NYCE.
While many softs traders had expressed alarm over the prospect of a takeover by the mammoth NYMEX, most were enthusiastic over the idea of shared quarters.
"No one wants to be bought by NYMEX, but they all want to be under one roof," another trader said.
CSCE trades futures and options contracts in coffee, cocoa, sugar and dairy products. Last year 11.5 million contracts were traded at the exchange.

The 137-year-old Cotton Exchange lists futures and options contracts in cotton, orange juice and other financial instruments including the U.S. Dollar Index, Treasury notes and U.S.-based currency contracts. In 1996, six million contracts were traded.
